en: The Theravāda Vinaya:
The Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga,
Chapter on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Robes 11.
The Training Rule on Heavy Outer Cloaks.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunī Thullanandā was learned, an eloquent speaker, confident, and skilled in delivering a discourse on the Dhamma.

Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having wrapped himself in a costly woolen blanket during the cold season, approached the bhikkhunī Thullanandā; having approached, he paid homage to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā and sat down to one side.
As King Pasenadi of Kosala was sitting there to one side, the bhikkhunī Thullanandā instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Then, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the bhikkhunī Thullanandā’s discourse on the Dhamma, King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to her:
“Venerable lady, please say whatever you need.”
“If you wish to give me something, Great King, give me this woolen blanket.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having given the woolen blanket to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, rose from his seat, paid homage to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, and keeping her to his right, departed.
People criticized, complained, and spread it about:
“These bhikkhunīs have great desires and are not content.
How can they request a woolen blanket from the king?
The bhikkhunīs heard those people grumbling, complaining, and spreading it about.
Those bhikkhunīs who were of few desires... they complained, grumbled, and spread it about:
"How can the noble lady Thullanandā request a woolen blanket from the king? ... [They asked:
"Is it true, monks, that the bhikkhunī Thullanandā requested a woolen blanket from the king?"
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked her:
“… How can the bhikkhunī Thullanandā request a woolen blanket from a king? …”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, the bhikkhunīs should recite this training rule thus:

‘If a bhikkhunī has a heavy cloak made, it should be made at most four karṣas in weight. If she should have it made for more than that, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).’”
"Garupāvuraṇaṃ" means any kind of cloak used during the cold season. "Cetāpentiyā" means [causing it to be] bought.
"By one who makes it known.
"It should be exchanged for up to four kaṁsas" means it should be exchanged for what is worth sixteen kahāpaṇas.
If she should cause it to be procured beyond that:
if she requests more than that, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the act;
upon acquisition, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
It must be relinquished to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to a single bhikkhunī.
And thus, monks, it should be relinquished:
…pe…
“Venerable ladies, this heavy cloak of mine, acquired for more than four *kaṃsa* [in weight], is subject to relinquishment; I relinquish it to the Saṅgha.
… “Let her give it” … “Let them give it” … [and so on].
"I give it to the noble lady.
If she causes [the cloth] to be sought while it is more than four spans in excess, and she perceives it as being more than that, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If she causes it to be sought while it is more than four spans in excess, but she is uncertain of it, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If she causes [a robe] to be made when it exceeds four finger-breadths [in width], perceiving it as less than that, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If it is less than four finger-breadths and she perceives it as exceeding that, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is less than four finger-breadths and she is doubtful about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she perceives it as less than four kaṁsas when it is less than four kaṁsas,
there is no offense.
There is no offense if she causes [the robe] to be procured for up to four kaṁsas.
If she causes [something] to be procured for [her] relatives or those who have invited her, and it does not exceed four kāsas in value;
If, for the sake of another,

one causes something of small value to be bartered for something of great value using one's own wealth; or, desiring to cause something of great value to be bartered, one causes something of small value to be bartered instead.
"Of one who is insane,
of one who is a first-offender.
The eleventh training rule is concluded.
